title: RubriQ: Rubric-Guided Group Relative Policy Optimization for Constraint-Aware Quantum Circuit Synthesis
abstract: Designing fault-tolerant quantum circuits that are both algorithmically correct and hardware compatible remains a major bottleneck in the transition to scalable quantum computing. We introduce RubriQ, a scalable framework that formulates circuit synthesis as a large language model (LLM) code-generation task, optimized via group relative policy optimization (GRPO). Unlike conventional black-box neural critics, RubriQ employs a domain-grounded programmatic rubric as the reinforcement learning reward function, evaluating circuits for T-gate reduction, hardware topology compliance, and unitary fidelity. To support high-throughput training, RubriQ integrates GPU-accelerated CUDA-Q simulation directly into the reinforcement learning (RL) loop and is deployed on NERSC Perlmutter using DeepSpeed ZeRO2 across multinode NVIDIA A100 clusters. On benchmark tasks, RubriQ achieves a mean T-gate compression of 3.31x, significantly outperforming sparse-reward RL baselines (2.05x), converging 2-3x faster, and maintaining less than 1\% hardware-constraint violations. Validated on IBM and IonQ quantum processors, RubriQ establishes an automated, high-performance computing (HPC)-driven pipeline for generating hardware-ready, fault-tolerant quantum circuits at scale.
summary: This paper introduces RubriQ, a novel framework that uses Large Language Models guided by a multi-dimensional programmatic rubric to synthesize hardware-ready, fault-tolerant quantum circuits. By optimizing via Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) and incorporating metrics like T-gate count and hardware topology directly into the reward function, it significantly outperforms existing methods in efficiency and fidelity.
main_problem: The primary challenge is designing fault-tolerant quantum circuits that are simultaneously algorithmically correct and compatible with specific physical hardware constraints.
main_result: RubriQ achieves a significant mean T-gate compression of 3.31x compared to baselines, converges faster, and maintains low hardware constraint violations on real quantum processors.
method: The authors developed RubriQ, which frames circuit synthesis as an LLM code-generation task optimized using Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO). The reward signal is derived from a programmatic rubric evaluating multiple physical constraints.
model_or_system: The system targets quantum circuits for fault-tolerant computation on platforms like superconducting qubits (IBM) and trapped ions (IonQ). It uses an LLM fine-tuned via LoRA to generate OpenQASM/Qiskit code, which is then parsed into a circuit.
key_observables: T-gate count compression ratio, hardware compliance score ($S_H$), Process Fidelity ($S_F$), Clifford fraction ($S_C$), and overall convergence speed (epochs).
important_parameters: The optimization uses five weighted components in the rubric reward function; $N=8$ is selected as the optimal group size for GRPO.
main_assumptions: The method assumes that a multi-dimensional, programmatic rubric can effectively guide policy learning without relying on complex learned critics. Theoretical analysis suggests weight adaptation might be needed at high circuit complexity ($T_0 > 140$).
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the full system architecture (three stages: prompt encoding, LLM generation, parsing) and compare hardware topologies to show how routing constraints impact the reward score.
paper_structure: The paper details the three-stage pipeline (LLM $ightarrow$ Parser $ightarrow$ Rubric Evaluation), introduces GRPO for policy updates using a weighted sum of five component scores ($R = w_C S_C + \dots$), and validates performance against baselines on real hardware backends.
why_interesting: While focused on quantum computation, the rigorous integration of physical constraints (topology, gate type) into an automated optimization loop provides a blueprint for designing complex quantum control sequences that must respect underlying physics.

figures.caption: Fig. 1. RubriQ system architecture. The three-stage pipeline converts a natural-language prompt (1. system with user prompt encoding) into executable circuit code (2. autoregressive LLM generation with low-rank adaptation (LoRA) [33]) and a validated quantum circuit object (3. multi-strategy extraction). The rubric scoring engine (grey dashed box) supplies dense, bounded, deterministic rewards across five dimensions and GRPO policy update (pink box) enables critic-free, scalable policy gradients using group normalization. The circuits are validated on IBM and IonQ hardware; the full pipeline runs on NERSC Perlmutter A100 clusters.

Fig. 2. Hardware topology comparison driving RubriQ compatibility score SH. Top: IBM Eagle/Heron heavy-hex lattice (degree ≤3); a CNOT between non-adjacent qubits q0 and q3 requires two SWAPs (6 extra two-qubit gates). Bottom: IonQ Forte/Aria all-to-all connectivity (degree = N−1); the same CNOT maps directly with zero routing overhead. RubriQ takes the maximum SH over backends, allowing the policy to discover backend-specific optimization strategies.

Fig. 3. Per-step GRPO training flow. A prompt yields N=8 completions; parse failures receive R=0. The rubric engine scores each valid circuit across five dimensions and aggregates Ri. Group-relative normalization produces advantages ˆ Ai without a learned critic. The bar chart shows how GRPO amplifies high-reward circuits (green, right) and suppresses failures (red, left); dense rubric scoring keeps within-group dispersion high, enabling accurate ranking.

Fig. 4. GPU-hours (A100) for a full training run as a function of circuit width, comparing RubriQ against Sparse-GRPO and Sparse-PPO. Solid lines: measured (nq≤8); dashed: projected (nq>8). Background bands indicate HPC configuration: 1 node with 4 A100s (nq=2–5), 2 nodes with 8 A100s (nq=6–8), 2+ nodes with 8+ A100s (nq>8). All three methods share the same per-epoch cost (dominated by O(4nq) fidelity simulation); the 2.6× gap reflects RubriQ faster convergence (15 vs. 40 epochs), directly translating to proportional GPU-hour savings at every qubit scale.
Fig. 5. (a) T-gate compression C=T0/T(c) vs. epoch by dataset. (b) Train- ing and validation MSE; overlap indicates LoRA regularization rather than overfitting.
